name: Liam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the returns department of a big online clothes warehouse, day shift, seven till half three. People send back jeans and dresses, and I open the bags, check for stains or tags cut off, grade each item A, B or C, and send it back to the shelves or to the outlet pile. On a busy Monday after a sale, it's mountains of grey bags as high as the cage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a bit of detective work, you find lipstick on collars and receipts in pockets, even a wedding ring once. What wears me out is standing at the bench all day and the targets, which are around ninety items an hour. My partner Sofia is a nurse on rotating shifts, so I do most of the cooking, and that's my wind-down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing, because people need jobs more than shareholders need another gadget. At work I'd joke that the scanner still can't tell a stain from a shadow. Online I mostly just like other people's posts, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but the company's struggling anyway. Online fashion is cut-throat, and they shut one site last year and moved the work here. So I'd still feel like the ground is a bit soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at returns and keep my union card active, because the union got us the sit-down breaks. Sofia and I want to put another hundred a month aside, so we've got four months saved instead of three. Maybe I'd look at evening classes, but not seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy. It's like nothing's on fire, but the smoke alarm battery is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company shut a site. What happened to the people there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred people lost their jobs in a town an hour away, and some of them came here on agency contracts. My mate Kofi on the next bench was one of them. He took a pay cut to come here, and he's still bitter about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most if hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, easily, because we're in a two-bed terrace and the landlord puts it up every year. Sofia's pay is steady, so we'd manage, but we'd stop going away in summer. That's the first thing that goes.

say: I'd say people need **jobs** more than shareholders need gadgets.
I'd joke at work that the scanner can't tell a **stain** from a shadow.
think: I'd be relieved, but the **company is struggling** in cut-throat online fashion.
They **shut a site** last year, so the ground still feels soft.
do: Keep working in **returns** and keep my **union card** active.
Save **another hundred** a month with Sofia to reach four months.
Glance at **evening classes**, but not seriously.
feel: Mostly fine but **uneasy**, like a smoke alarm with a **low battery**.
S0.quote: Nothing's on fire, but the smoke alarm battery is low.
fieldNote: His worry comes from a **struggling employer**, not from AI.
He credits the **union** with real gains like sit-down breaks.
A steady partner's income makes the **rent** pressure manageable.
He watched **Kofi**, a colleague, take a pay cut after a site closure.

steps.text: Keep grading clothing returns on the day shift
Save an extra hundred a month with Sofia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies are using AI to squeeze workers and the union has to have a say in how it's used. I'd post about it, actually, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, returns is half thinking work. Deciding if a dress is grade A or B is exactly the kind of checking AI could do with a camera. They've already trialled one. So my bench could shrink to people just opening bags while the camera decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools they bring in and get good at them, because being the guy who knows the system keeps you on. I'd ask the union rep about the company's retraining fund. And I'd start looking properly at an electrician apprenticeship, because my uncle's an electrician and says they're short of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yeah. Not panicking, because Sofia's job is safe and I've got options, but my stomach drops when I think about the camera trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about that camera trial.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they put a camera over one bench, and it photographed every item and suggested a grade. It got about eight out of ten right, and the supervisor said that was good enough for cheap stuff. The bench person still had to open the bags, but the grading was the bit that made the job interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI tools. Do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, I used one to tidy up a cover letter last year and to plan a holiday. I'm not a tech guy, I wait until everyone's using something. But if the company's going that way, I'd rather be in front than behind.

say: I'd say the **union** must have a say in how companies use AI.
I'd actually **post online** about AI being used to squeeze workers.
think: Grading clothes is **checking work** that an AI camera could do.
My bench could shrink to **just opening bags** while the camera decides.
do: Learn the company's **AI grading tools** and become the one who knows them.
Ask the union rep about the **retraining fund**.
Look seriously at an **electrician apprenticeship** through my uncle.
feel: **Anxious**, with his stomach dropping about the **camera trial**.
Steadied by Sofia's **secure job** and having options.
S1.quote: Deciding if a dress is grade A or B is exactly the kind of checking AI could do with a camera.
fieldNote: He spots that **grading returns** is thinking work, so Steady Disruption hits him early.
A real **camera trial** at his site makes the threat concrete.
He would **learn the tools** to stay useful, typical of a steady adopter.
His **uncle's trade** gives him a realistic exit path.

steps.text: Learn the AI grading camera and become the bench expert
Ask the union rep about the company retraining fund
Apply for an electrician apprenticeship through his uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, or something like it, because there won't be enough work to go round. I'd be at the protests and I'd be posting every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the grading goes almost straight away in 2028, because that's pure thinking work. Then I'm a bag-opener for three years until the robots come in 2031. I'd be out of returns before I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship the first year, even on apprentice pay, and we'd live on Sofia's wage plus savings. I'd cut the car, because we can get by on buses. And I'd join the union campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight thinking about it, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would being an electrician be safe if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I think rewiring an old house is about the last thing a robot will manage, all those crooked walls and surprises. But I wouldn't bet my life on it, I'd just be betting a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sofia say to each other about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down at the kitchen table with a spreadsheet, which Sofia loves. I think Sofia (his partner) would say she can carry us for a year, and I'd hate that, but I'd take it. Pride doesn't pay the rent.

say: I'd say this is the moment for a **basic income**.
I'd be at the **protests** and posting every day.
think: **Grading** goes almost straight away in 2028 because it's thinking work.
I'd be a **bag-opener** until robots arrive in 2031, out before thirty.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** in the first year on apprentice pay.
Sell the **car** and get by on buses.
Join the union campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a tight chest because **two years** is nothing.
S2.quote: I think Sofia (his partner) would say she can carry us for a year, and I'd hate that, but I'd take it. Pride doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking part** of his job going in 2028, before robots.
He'd accept **apprentice pay** and lean on Sofia, overriding his pride.
He's honest that an electrician job only buys **a few more years**.
His politics sharpen into a call for **basic income**.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship on apprentice pay
Sell the car and use buses to cut costs
Join the union campaign for a basic income
Live on Sofia's nursing wage while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up proper retraining, paid for by the companies making the money. I'd keep saying it at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd think the grading goes around 2031 and the bag-opening around 2034. That's long enough to finish an apprenticeship properly and get a couple of years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my returns job for now and save hard for a year, so we've got six months saved before I drop to apprentice pay. Then I'd start the electrician course in 2028. I'd also learn whatever AI tools electricians use, because my uncle says even quoting jobs is going on apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the useful kind. It gets me moving instead of freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to your uncle. Who is he to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncle Ray (his mother's brother) has been an electrician for thirty years and always said there's a place for me. I never took him up on it because I liked having mates at the warehouse. With five years' warning, I'd finally ring Uncle Ray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The jokes on the bench and the weird stuff in pockets. Kofi and I have a running list of the strangest finds. You don't get that wiring sockets on your own.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to set up proper retraining.
Retraining should be **paid for** by the companies making the money.
think: Grading goes around **2031** and bag-opening around **2034**.
That's long enough to finish an **apprenticeship** and get a couple of years in.
do: Keep the returns job and save until we have **six months** put by.
Learn the **AI apps** electricians use for quoting.
feel: **Anxious** in a useful way that gets him **moving**.
S3.quote: Uncle Ray (his mother's brother) has been an electrician for thirty years and always said there's a place for me.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan into a **timed sequence**: save, then train.
He would miss the **social side** of the warehouse most.
Family ties through **Uncle Ray** give him a concrete exit.
He'd learn **AI quoting apps**, picking tools up once they're proven.

steps.text: Save hard for a year to reach six months of expenses
Start an electrician course with Uncle Ray in 2028
Learn the AI quoting apps electricians use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to get it right, so no excuses for the government or the companies. I'd say it calmly at work and in the union chat, though, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a gift for someone like me. Robots don't come for returns until about 2039, and by then I could be a fully qualified electrician with my own van. I'd still worry about Kofi and the older people who can't switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in returns for two or three more years and save toward six months. Then I'd do the apprenticeship around 2029, while I'm still in my early thirties. Meanwhile I'd keep going to union meetings to push for a retraining fund for the people who stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried. It feels like enough time to land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said electrician only buys a few more years. Does that still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. Even in 2039 there'll be robots that can wire a new-build, maybe. But forty with a trade, savings and a nurse for a partner beats forty with nothing but a grading bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kofi (his workmate) to start something now, while he's got ten years, and not wait for the company to tell him. He won't listen, he never does. But I'd say it.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for government or companies.
I'd say it **calmly** at work and in the union chat, not shouting.
think: Ten years is **a gift**: I could be a qualified electrician with a **van**.
I'd still worry about **Kofi** and older workers who can't switch.
do: Stay in returns two or three years and **save** toward six months.
Keep pushing the union for a **retraining fund**.
S4.quote: Forty with a trade, savings and a nurse for a partner beats forty with nothing but a grading bench.
fieldNote: The long warning turns his fear into a **workable plan**.
He still doubts any trade is **safe forever**.
His concern shifts to **colleagues** who won't move.
He would keep the **union** fight going for those who stay.

steps.text: Save toward six months while staying in returns
Push the union branch for a retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be learning a trade at the same moment everyone else is. What would help is paid retraining, a wage you can live on while you do an apprenticeship, not apprentice pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my partner. Sofia's job feels safe in every picture, and that's the only reason I'm not panicking. If you're single in this job, I think it's much scarier.

headlineQuote: If you're single in this job, I think it's much scarier.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old returns grader** at a large online clothing warehouse.
He lives with **Sofia**, a nurse, and they have three to four months saved.
He's a quiet **union supporter** who uses AI now and then and adopts tech once proven.
He sees **grading returns** as thinking work that AI could take early.
His exit plan is an **electrician apprenticeship** with Uncle Ray, timed to the warning he gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be retraining at the same time as everyone else.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a living wage during an apprenticeship.
